content_list.content_text: It had an individual viewer through which, by inserting a coin, one could watch a short strip of film playing in a loop, showing moving images of comedy acts, trained animals and dancers.

The films played in the Kinetoscope were produced with the Kinetograph, another invention patented by Thomas Edison. Although these inventions remain in Edison's name, they were actually produced by William K.L. Dickson and a team of technicians tasked by Edison with creating machines that would produce and display moving photographs (motion pictures). In 1889, Edison decided to create the camera described when he saw Étienne-Jules Marey's camera in Paris.

content_list.content_text: A close-up, or simply a close, in film and audiovisual media, is a type of shot characterized by its tight framing, showing only part of the object or subject being filmed, usually a person's face.

information.contentTitle: The Art of Close-Ups with Edgar Wright

content_list.content_text: It can be achieved by moving the camera very close to the object or character, or by using a lens with a narrow angle of view (and therefore a long focal length). First used in English in 1913, the term close-up is synonymous with close shot, big close shot and tight shot.

Its origin lies in the double meaning of the word close, which in English means both to shut (to close) and near (close to). By analogy, the term also came to be used in other visual arts, such as photography, comics and even painting, to describe still images with tight framing, most particularly of the human face.

content_list.content_text: The Hays Code (officially the Motion Picture Production Code) was a set of moral guidelines applied by the major film studios to films released in the United States between 1930 and 1968. It was named after Will H. Hays, a Presbyterian lawyer and politician and president of the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America (MPPDA) from 1922 to 1945. Under Hays's leadership, the MPPDA (later known as the MPAA) adopted a self-censorship code in 1930, which was enforced more strictly from 1934 onward.

information.contentTitle: The Motion Pictures Production Code logo

content_list.content_text: This code spelled out which content was acceptable or unacceptable for films produced in the United States. Between 1934 and 1954, the Hays Code was closely identified with Joseph Breen, the administrator appointed by Hays to enforce the code as head of the Production Code Administration (PCA). The film industry followed the code to the letter until 1956, when, due to the impact of television, the influence of foreign films and the intervention of the Supreme Court, the code underwent slight changes. As a result of the 1960s counterculture, several filmmakers began deliberately violating the code. In 1964, Sidney Lumet included scenes of nude women in The Pawnbroker. It was one of the first American films to feature nudity, and although the MPAA had insisted it was an exception, other directors soon began to defy the Hays Code, which was replaced in 1968 by the MPAA's film rating system, still in effect today.

Films that complied with the code received an MPAA seal of approval, while those that failed were barred from distribution by the organization, which greatly reduced their reach with audiences and their chances of commercial success. In addition, offending studios were fined 25,000 dollars. To this day the MPAA grants a seal to films distributed by its member studios; today, however, the seal carries the work's age rating, which can be G (suitable for all ages), PG (some material may not be suitable for children), PG-13 (some material may be inappropriate for children under 13), R (under 17 requires an accompanying adult) or NC-17 (adult content — no one 17 and under admitted).

content_list.content_text: The film director is the professional responsible for turning an idea or screenplay into a production (for film or television), coordinating its execution. A film director takes on the functions of art direction, cinematography, lighting, animation and staging.

information.contentTitle: Quentin Tarantino Explains How to Write & Direct Movies | The Director’s Chair

content_list.content_text: A film director's responsibilities include defining the overall artistic direction that will characterize the film as a whole; selecting the actors and technical crew; discussing the budget and schedule with the production manager; directing rehearsals and shoots, recordings or stagings, setting the actors' blocking and the technical crew's work; guiding the actors' work, determining gestures, tone of voice, facial expression and all the details essential to building the characters; guiding the camera operators' work, determining camera movements and shots; approving locations, sets, costumes, lighting and soundtrack; directing and supervising the editing, dubbing, the making of the score or soundtrack and all the editing of the film up to the final print; supervising the editing work for TV; following the production of trailers and promotional pieces; and analyzing and interpreting the film's screenplay, adapting it for filmmaking. To perform well as a film director, it is essential to be patient and persevering, a perfectionist, and to have artistic sensitivity and a critical sense.

content_list.content_text: German Expressionism was a film style that peaked in the 1920s, characterized by the distortion of sets and characters, through makeup, photographic techniques and other devices, in order to express the way the filmmakers saw the world.

information.contentTitle: German Expressionism: Crash Course Film

content_list.content_text: Expressionism, whose origins can be traced back to strong evidence in Van Gogh, spread across almost all the arts, such as film and painting, and is characterized by the distortion of the image (the use of vibrant colors evocative of the supernatural), a return to the Gothic and opposition to a society immersed in the bleak landscape of modern rationalism, which preached mechanical labor. The vibrant, hallucinatory paintings express a detachment from reality, the primacy of the "self" and its personal vision of the world.

This identity as an art of crisis intensified as it coincided with the establishment of the fragile Weimar Republic after a catastrophic lost war and a humiliating Treaty of Versailles, which ruined the German nation; this helped shape not only a new aesthetic stance but also an ethos of defiance toward authority (which is why the Nazis considered Expressionism a degenerate art). Nazism and World War II itself destroyed many of these works.

content_list.content_text: Film noir (French pronunciation: [film nwaʁ]; literally 'black film') is a French expression designating a subgenre of crime film, derived from the suspense novel and influenced by German Expressionism, which peaked in the United States between 1939 and 1950.

information.contentTitle: What Is Film Noir?

content_list.content_text: The expression was first applied to a film by French critic Nino Frank in 1946, by analogy with the crime novels of the Série noire, a collection created by Gallimard in 1945 whose books had black and yellow covers, with a black dust jacket and white borders. The expression was unknown to directors and actors at the time the classic films noirs were produced, having been introduced later by film historians and critics. Many of the creators of films noirs later revealed that they had no idea, at the time, that they had given rise to a film subgenre.

Noir derives from the suspense novels of the Great Depression era (many were adapted from crime novels of the period) and from the aesthetics of 1930s horror films. The first noirs appeared in the early 1940s. Historically, they were shot in high-contrast black and white, under the influence of German Expressionist cinematography.

content_list.content_text: Film genre is the means used to distinguish the various types of films, in a classification derived from literary studies, and it serves as a useful tool for analyzing world cinema.

information.contentTitle: What are film genres?

content_list.content_text: For Graeme Turner, film genre thus follows a system of codes, conventions and visual styles that allow viewers to identify, quickly and with some complexity, what kind of plot they are watching; the purpose of this division, according to him, is to make films more understandable and familiar to audiences, telling them in advance what to expect from the narrative, although nuances may be perceived along the way that qualify the work as also belonging to other genres or subgenres.

Genre thus includes scenes that are expected from a work that fits within it (for example: a car race, a shootout); this can have negative effects, such as making the work too predictable; likewise, the lack of fit within a specific genre can make a film incomprehensible to audiences and lead it to box office failure (as in the case of Francis Ford Coppola's One from the Heart, which not only mixes several genres but also blends fiction and reality); genre thus emerges almost as a determinism inherent to the mass media, again according to Turner.

Genres also change over time; they evolve from a classical form until they come to take on the role of parody and challenge to the genre itself — the Western being a prime example. Turner argues that genre is shaped by the convergence of three elements: the pressure of the film industry, the expectations of the audience and, finally, the text that underpins it.

content_list.content_text: High-definition video is a technology that makes it possible to shoot with a quality similar to that of motion picture film stock, which was widely used from the birth of cinema until the end of the 2010s.

2D high-definition video can convey a perception of depth as long as it is shown on a suitable television set. Video in this format takes into account the recording medium (which may be optical or magnetic), its encoding (analog or digital), the aspect ratio (4:3 or 16:9), the number of lines per frame (720 or 1080), and even the system developed by the market's leading brands (Arri Alexa, HDDV, CineAlta, etc.).

Internationally accepted standards for "broadcasting" (free-to-air TV transmission) are the subject of constant disputes and have yet to reach a consensus. Beyond capture systems, one must also take into account the systems used for broadcast or home viewing.

Using proper cabling to connect receivers, monitors and television sets, such as HDMI cables, allows for final viewing with above-average brightness, contrast, sharpness, luminance and chrominance (image sampling). "Full HD" refers to any system with at least 1080 lines, a 16:9 aspect ratio (at least 1920 x 1080 pixels), progressive or interlaced scanning, and a rate of 25 or 30 frames per second.

Image Maximum (IMAX) is a film format created by the Canadian company IMAX Corporation that can display images far larger in size and resolution than conventional film exhibition systems. A standard IMAX screen is 22 meters (72 feet) wide and 16.1 meters (52.8 feet) tall, but screens can be larger. In 2008, IMAX became the most widely used system for large-format and special film presentations. As of March 2007, there were 280 IMAX theaters in 39 countries (60% of them located in Canada and the United States).

information.contentTitle: The Canadian origins of IMAX

content_list.content_text: Half of these theaters are commercial and half are educational. In September 2014, the total number of IMAX screens in the US passed the 400 mark. Variations on the traditional IMAX format include IMAX Dome (180º projection, with a different theater geometry), IMAX 3D and IMAX Digital. The largest IMAX Dome screen in the world is at Big Cinemas IMAX in Mumbai, India, with a screen area of 1,180 m2 (12,700 square feet). The largest rectangular IMAX screen in the world is located at the IMAX Theatre Sydney in Sydney, Australia, measuring 1,051 m2 (11,315 square feet), and is also equipped to show films.
The resolution of standard multiplex IMAX is 4K adjusted to look larger; specialized venues have a resolution of 10,000 by 7,000 pixels, and films can be produced on 35 mm or 70 mm.

content_list.content_text: A jump cut is a cut in video or film editing that removes part of a take, creating two shots and an abrupt transition between them. This type of editing creates the effect of jumping forward in time within the chronology of a scene or video.

information.contentTitle: How to Edit Videos with Jump Cuts

content_list.content_text: In filmmaking, its purpose is to move an action, or its cause, forward. It became popular among online content creators, commonly called "vloggers," as a way to shorten their videos or skip the speaker's pauses.

It is used to manipulate the narrative's space and time, taking the duration of a single take and fracturing it to move the audience forward, disregarding the usual regard for continuity, and thus often unsettling the audience. However, it is not considered something negative in a film production when used properly, at suitable moments that help the audience understand the story. Today this cut has taken on a new guise in its range of uses, appearing constantly in productions made for the internet, popularly known as "vlogs."

In these, the speaker is frequently cut, and the audience is always carried along an almost uninterrupted flow of the subject at hand. It became popular in this segment for several reasons, one of them decisive: the need to get the idea across in a minimal amount of time; another factor is the engagement of young people, who always pay more attention to things that are strangely random, so the editing follows that same logic. Another purpose of the jump cut is to minimize mistakes and flaws in an audiovisual project in order to make it as professional as possible. Jump cuts do not involve long pauses between cuts, since that would make the audience lose track of the subject. Some experts describe this technique as "hard cuts" and interpret and contextualize them by likening them to "opening and closing your eyes," as if a person watching the video needed to blink, a natural and necessary action for any human being.

content_list.content_text: Also known as the key light, front light or primary light, it is the most important of the three lights, positioned in front of the person being filmed. It defines the basic lighting of the scene. Most of the time, a direct, concentrated light is used here (the kind of light called hard light), which on its own (when it is the only light on) casts pronounced shadows on the person's face. In some cases, however, diffuse, scattered lighting (the kind of light called soft light) may be used instead, which casts almost no shadows. Hard light comes directly from the lamp, while soft light is obtained by using softening devices such as a diffuser placed in front of the lamp, or a softbox (that box of translucent material with the lamp inside).

Whether the key light produced by the lamp is hard or soft is chosen according to the atmosphere one wants to give the character in the scene. While soft light conveys a sense of calm and serenity by reducing visible lines on the face, hard light heightens the drama by emphasizing the shape, texture and relief of the filmed person's facial expressions. It also serves to emphasize their age, since wrinkles and imperfections are highlighted. Except in situations where the aim is to convey a mysterious, dramatic air, a soft key light is generally the best and most pleasing option.

content_list.content_text: Montage, or editing, is a process of selecting, ordering and adjusting the shots of a film or other audiovisual product in order to achieve the desired result, whether in narrative, informational, dramatic, visual or experimental terms, among others. In general, editing is done by the editor, on equipment compatible with the technology used to make the product, under the supervision of the director or, in some cases, the producer.

information.contentTitle: Top 10 Best Montages of All Time

content_list.content_text: Because it takes place after filming, editing is a post-production process, and for a long time it was considered the only process original to cinema, the thing that would make cinema an art or a language distinct from all others. Today, however, several authors argue that there are many similarities between editing and the processes of composition in other art forms, such as poetry or the novel.

A film editor at work in 1946. Film editing is both a creative and a technical part of the post-production process of filmmaking. The term derives from the traditional process of working with film, which increasingly involves the use of digital technology. The film editor works with the raw footage, selecting shots and combining them into sequences that create a finished motion picture. Film editing is described as an art or skill, the only art that is unique to cinema, setting filmmaking apart from the art forms that preceded it, although there are close parallels to the editing process in other art forms such as poetry and the novel. Film editing is often referred to as the "invisible art" because, when it is well practiced, the viewer can become so engaged that they are not aware of the editor's work.

On its most fundamental level, film editing is the art, technique and practice of assembling shots into a coherent sequence. The job of an editor is not simply to mechanically put pieces of a film together, cut off film slates or edit dialogue scenes. A film editor must work creatively with the layers of images, story, dialogue, music, pacing, as well as the actors' performances, to effectively "re-imagine" and even rewrite the film to craft a cohesive whole. Editors usually play a dynamic role in the making of a film. Sometimes, auteurist film directors edit their own films, for example Akira Kurosawa, Bahram Beyzai and the Coen brothers. With the advent of digital editing, film editors and their assistants have become responsible for many areas of filmmaking that used to be the responsibility of others.

information.contentTitle: The Perfect Montage of Parasite

content_list.content_text: For instance, in past years, picture editors dealt only with just that: the picture. Sound, music and (more recently) visual effects editors dealt with the practicalities of other aspects of the editing process, usually under the direction of the picture editor and the director. However, digital systems have increasingly put these responsibilities on the picture editor. It is common, especially on lower-budget films, for the editor to sometimes cut in temporary music, mock up visual effects and add temporary sound effects or other sound substitutes. These temporary elements are usually replaced by more refined final elements produced by the sound, music and visual effects teams hired to complete the picture.

Its leading figures were Roberto Rossellini, Vittorio De Sica and Luchino Visconti, all strongly influenced by the films of the French poetic realism school.

Italian Neorealist cinema was characterized by the use of elements of reality in a work of fiction, coming close at times, in some scenes, to the characteristics of documentary film. Unlike traditional fiction filmmaking, Neorealism sought to portray the social and economic reality of its time.

content_list.content_text: Nickelodeons (from American English nickel = a 5¢ coin, and Greek odeion = roofed theater) were a type of small, primitive movie theater of the early 20th century. In places where competition was greater, they often had a piano or an organ, on which the pianist or organist played whatever music they deemed appropriate for each scene (for example, classic ragtime during a chase scene, or what was known at the time as "Eliza-crossing-the-ice" music during the scariest moments).

information.contentTitle: Nickelodeon – By the way film History

content_list.content_text: The name "Nickelodeon" was coined by Harry Davis and John P. Harris, who opened their small theater by that name on Smithfield Street in Pittsburgh in June 1905. Although it was not the first theater in the world dedicated to showing films, Davis and Harris were so successful that their concept of continuous five-cent shows was quickly imitated by hundreds of entrepreneurs, who also copied the theater's original name.

Louis B. Mayer witnessed this explosion of nickelodeon theaters. He renovated the "Gem Theater" in Haverhill, converting it into a nickelodeon that opened in 1907 under the name "Orpheum Theater," and announced that it would be the venue for the moving pictures and illustrated songs of the Miles Brothers.
Nickelodeons gradually disappeared as cities expanded and the industry brought about the consolidation of larger, more comfortable movie theaters better suited to showing films.

content_list.content_text: Pre-Code Hollywood was a period in the American film industry between the introduction of sound, in the late 1920s, and the enforcement of the Motion Picture Production Code, which set out the censorship guidelines.

information.contentTitle: Pre-Code Hollywood

content_list.content_text: From 1934 on, the Motion Picture Production Code came to be called, incorrectly, the "Hays Code." Although the code was adopted in 1930, oversight was poor, which is why it was not strictly enforced until July 1, 1934. Before that date, film content was restricted more by local laws, negotiations between the Studio Relations Committee and the major studios, and popular opinion than by the Hays Code, which Hollywood producers very often ignored.

As a result, in the late 1920s and early 1930s, films included sexual innuendo, miscegenation, illegal drug use, infidelity, abortion, intense violence and homosexuality. The figure of the femme fatale dominated films such as Female, Baby Face and Red-Headed Woman, while the gangsters of The Public Enemy, Little Caesar and Scarface seemed more like heroes than villains. Besides femme fatale characters, films showed aspects of women's nature that would not be revisited until much later. Villainous characters profited from their actions, sometimes without major repercussions, and drug use was the main plot of several films. Pre-Code films were shorter than today's: they ran a little over an hour. Many of Hollywood's biggest stars, such as Clark Gable, Barbara Stanwyck and Edward G. Robinson, took their first steps in this era. However, other stars who triumphed at that time, such as Ruth Chatterton, Lyle Talbot and Warren William (considered "the king of Pre-Code"), fell into obscurity. From late 1933 through the first half of 1934, the Catholic clergy in the United States launched a campaign against what it considered "the immorality of American cinema." This, together with the social research of the time (which indicated that so-called "bad" films could encourage bad behavior) and the possibility that the government would take control of film censorship, applied the pressure needed for the studios to accept greater oversight.

content_list.content_text: A film producer is the film professional who works on the business side. The producer raises funds for a project they have developed themselves or for the company that hired them. They are involved in the project from conception to completion. It is the producer who initiates, coordinates, supervises and controls matters such as fundraising and hiring the workforce. The producer is basically the concrete foundation on which film creation rests.

There are different ways for a producer to get involved in a given project. In most cases, the executive producer is the owner of the production company that receives a co-production proposal from a director who has an original screenplay. Alternatively, the producer buys the adaptation rights to a literary work, invests in the work of an adapter (screenwriter) and puts the project together.

Their story, their journey and their process of transformation (or lack thereof) form the main structure of the entire plot. The protagonist usually carries the story's point of view.

content_list.content_text: The protagonist, in and of itself, has no value attached to it; they can be good or bad, moral or immoral. content_list.content_text: The screenplay, or script, is the written form of any audiovisual work, written by one or more professionals called screenwriters.

information.contentTitle: Mastering the Screenplay: Exposition in Film

content_list.content_text: The screenplay, or script, is a narrative document used as a guideline for films, television programs or video games. Fiction screenplays contain the entirety of a film or of an episode of a soap opera or series, divided into numbered scenes that describe the characters and the settings.

The screenplay includes all the dialogue, with directions for the actors regarding tone of voice and body language. It also states the time of day at which each scene takes place ("Day," "Night," "Sunset," "Dawn," etc.) and whether the scene is "Exterior" (shot outdoors) or "Interior" (shot in a studio). And when this occurs it is called "ambu." Non-fiction productions, such as the Oscars ceremony or the Criança Esperança telethon, also depend on a screenplay, as do documentaries and commercials. Each has its own language. The shooting script, developed later, gives directions regarding camera placement, use of cranes, lighting and audiovisual effects.

It is prepared by the director of the production, together with the technical crew and, occasionally, the screenwriter. In the dialogue, the screenwriter may indicate the character's tone with notes such as "curt," "cheerful," "surprised," etc. Nowadays, however, the screenwriter's interference in the actor's work, which is guided by the director, is kept to the necessary minimum. A complete absence of these indications, however, can lead to misreadings of a line's intentions. The characters' 'invisible' emotions are not spelled out in screenplays because they need to be shown to the viewer through the actors' lived actions in front of the camera. Hence the notion, essential to screenwriters, that "writing is describing."

information.contentTitle: Whiplash vs. Black Swan - The Anatomy of the Obsessed Artist

content_list.content_text: The emotions the viewer feels from the stimulus of a scene in a film result from the interpretation of the different events described in the screenplay that take place in front of the camera, such as actions and movements. In semiotic terms, one could say that the scene contains cues for the viewer, who needs to decode and interpret what is shown. A screenplay in which the described actions follow one another and convey a meaning through the set of actions as a whole is a good screenplay. Dramatic works intended for the theater are not called 'screenplays,' nor is the outline followed in a newscast. The former are simply called "plays," and the latter is known in technical jargon as the rundown.

content_list.content_text: A special effect is any of various techniques used in the entertainment, film and television industries to create scenes that cannot be achieved by normal means or through live action.

information.contentTitle: How Are Special Effects Made?

content_list.content_text: These techniques are also used when creating effects by traditional means would be prohibitively expensive; for example, it would be extremely costly to build a 16th-century castle or sink a 20th-century ocean liner, but this can be simulated with visual effects. With the advent of computer graphics, they are also used to enhance previously filmed elements, adding, removing or highlighting objects in a scene.

There are many different special effects techniques, ranging from traditional theatrical effects (such as those of the English "Restoration spectacles" of the late 17th century), through the classic cinematic techniques invented in the early 20th century, such as aerial photography and optical printing, to modern computer graphics. Different techniques are often used together in a single scene or shot to achieve the desired effect.

information.contentTitle: Designing Tim Burton’s Dumbo – Visual Effects Masterclass

list.title: VFX in Netflix’s Mindhunter: Matte Paintings, Composites, and 3D Tracking

content_list.content_text: A widescreen display is a television screen or monitor, or a projection (of film or another medium), whose ratio between the width and height of the active screen area (the one that displays the image) is greater than that of the classic Pythagorean 4:3 format (1.3[3] = 1.333...). This means that for every 1 cm of height, the image is about 1.33 cm wide.
The best-known widescreen formats are 1.77:1 (16:9), 2.33:1 (21:9) and 2.66:1 (CinemaScope). The latter format is most common in movie theaters and commercial film projection.

Photographic film (sometimes shortened to film), used in photography, consists of a flexible, transparent plastic base, usually cellulose triacetate, on which a photographic emulsion is deposited. This emulsion is a thin layer of gelatin containing crystals of silver salts that are sensitive to the light reaching them through the camera lens.

Silver salts, chemically known as silver halides, can be more or less sensitive to light. Thus, some films require a greater amount of light to record images, while others allow images to be captured with less light. This property is called sensitivity.

list.title: Film stock
list.subtitle: Wikipedia

content_list.content_text: Serials, also called film serials, movie serials or chapter plays, are sequential films with a limited number of short episodes that together form a complete story, which were shown in movie theaters during the first half of the 20th century.

information.contentTitle: At This Theater Next Week! Remembering Movie Serials

content_list.content_text: Serials are now considered a form of B movie, not only because they were based on simplified formulas, but also because they were made on low budgets and aimed mainly at profit, traits associated with the B movie. They usually had between 10 and 15 episodes, with some exceptions, and each episode ended on an extreme note, with the hero (or heroine) facing a dangerous, seemingly hopeless situation, so as to hold the audience's attention, make them curious to see the next episode and find out how the danger would be overcome, a device that became known in film as the cliffhanger. The episodes were originally weekly, and always ended with an invitation to the audience to see the next one.

The story told by the serial, explains William Henckemaier, usually involved a hero or heroine fighting evil, against some villain who continually exposed them to traps or extremely dangerous situations, from which the hero bravely escaped. The final moment of an episode often implied the hero's death or defeat, but in the following episode the audience saw them survive through persistence and courage. The situation was repeated throughout the serial, in a sequence of continuous traps and dangers, until finally, in the last episode, the hero defeated the villain. The characters were highly caricatured and archetypal, representing heroes and villains, and there was usually a “best friend,” a sidekick who served as support for the main character.

list.title: Serial Films
list.subtitle: filmsite.org

list.title: Serial Films

content_list.content_text: The epic, in the cinematic sense, is a genre that portrays tales of great heroes, centered entirely on a single main character or on a people. Epics typically feature large-scale productions and dramatic themes, making for a grand spectacle. The use of the term has changed over time; sometimes it designates a film genre, and other times it is simply a synonym for a big-budget film.

information.contentTitle: Top 5 Historical Epics of All Time

content_list.content_text: These films follow the classical literary sense, focusing on a heroic character. The ambitious nature of an epic helps define it and set it apart from other types of film, such as period pieces or adventure films. Epic films usually recount a historical or mythical event, with extravagant sets and lavish costumes, accompanied by a striking score and a large cast, which tends to make them among the most expensive films ever produced. The most common subjects of epic films are warriors, gladiators and/or figures from various periods of world history. Besides historical films, fantasy films such as The Lord of the Rings and Star Wars also incorporate the aforementioned elements of epic cinema.

list.title: Epic Cinema
list.subtitle: mnemocine.com

list.title: Epic Film
list.subtitle: Wikipedia

content_list.content_text: A tracking shot (travelling), in film and audiovisual terminology, is any camera movement in which the camera actually moves through space - as opposed to panning movements, in which the camera merely rotates on its own axis without moving.

information.contentTitle: Directing Camera Movement — Filmmaking Techniques for Directors

content_list.content_text: The term travelling can also refer to the type of equipment used to achieve such movements. In most situations, the tracking shot is achieved by moving the camera with the help of a cart on rails, which allows smoother movement over any kind of terrain. This type of equipment (cart + rails) is also called a travelling.

When the floor is more even, a cart with tires, usually called a dolly, can be used; it has the advantage of being able to move in any direction, not just along the rails. Handheld camera moves are also considered tracking shots, as are movements using cranes or camera stabilizers such as the Steadicam - as long as, during the shot, the camera actually moves through space rather than merely rotating on its horizontal or vertical axis (which would make it a pan).

list.title: Filmmaking techniques: Directing the camera

content_list.content_text: A vamp is an archetype of a seductive, attractive woman who is usually also perverse and cruel. Unlike the femme fatale, however, the vamp is not necessarily a criminal or a murderer, but she has traits of coldness and sadism. The vamp is also described as a mysterious woman, glamorous in an exotic and stylized way. In pop culture, the vamp is also associated with sadomasochism.

information.contentTitle: The Silent Vamps

content_list.content_text: The conventional vamp wears dark clothes, has dark hair and uses contrasting makeup that heightens her pallor and accentuates her eyes and lips, giving her a dark, gothic look. In Hollywood films, vamps were often foreigners, originally from Eastern Europe or Asia, and were sometimes considered the opposite of gamines. Famous vamps of silent film included Theda Bara, Louise Glaum, Musidora, Nita Naldi, Pola Negri and Myrna Loy (early in her career).

list.title: Femme fatale
list.subtitle: Wikipedia

list.title: Silent Film and the Vamps
list.subtitle: blogosanosperdidos.com

content_list.content_text: It girl is a term used to refer to women who, even unintentionally, set trends and spark people's interest in the way they dress, walk, think or are. As a rule, “it girls” have what many call “charisma,” something that draws attention to them.

Their most defining trait is being unusual, standing out from ordinary people and arousing interest, to the point that others start copying the way they dress, speak and/or act. “It girls” usually behave irreverently and make people curious about their way of life. The male version of the expression "it girl" is "it boy."

The first use of the concept of "it" in this sense can be found in a story by Rudyard Kipling: "'Tisn't beauty, so to speak, nor good talk necessarily. It's just 'It'." Elinor Glyn said in a lecture: "With 'It' you win all men if you are a woman and all women if you are a man. 'It' can be a quality of the mind as well as a physical attraction."

The expression drew worldwide attention in 1927 with the film It, starring Clara Bow. Many "it girls" have some connection to the arts world, such as actresses, singers, models, etc. Some, in the fashion world, bring runway trends into everyday life, compelling women to follow the same style.

list.title: It girl
list.subtitle: Wikipedia

content_list.content_text: A femme fatale (originally a French term) is a female archetype or stock character widely used in crime literature and film and in European drama. The femme fatale usually seduces and deceives the hero and other men to obtain something they would not freely give.

information.contentTitle: The Femme Fatale Trope, Explained

content_list.content_text: Although typically villains, femmes fatales can also be antiheroines in certain stories, and sometimes they even repent and end up becoming heroines. Today, the archetype is generally seen as a character who constantly crosses the line between good and evil, acting unscrupulously regardless of social norms and any open commitments she has to the hero. She is usually presented as a counterpoint to the ingénue.

In social life, the femme fatale torments her partner in an asymmetrical relationship, withholding confirmation of her affection, let alone the opposite, to the point where the man becomes obsessed, addicted and exhausted, and unable to make rational decisions or manage his own personal life.

list.title: Femme fatale
list.subtitle: Wikipedia

content_list.content_text: Stop motion, or frame-by-frame, is an animation technique widely used with the help of a photographic camera or a computer. Real models made of various materials are used, the most common being tree wood with trunks and modeling clay. In film, the material used has to be more durable and malleable, since the models need to last for months, as the fashion events for each one cause different wear. Not all stop-motion animation consists only of objects; human actors can also be used. Approximately 24 frames are needed to create one second of animation. Depending on the process, 600 or more photos of the performers are taken.

information.contentTitle: How Stop-Motion Movies Are Animated At The Studio Behind 'Missing Link'

content_list.content_text: The models are moved and photographed frame by frame. These frames are later assembled onto film stock, creating the impression of movement. At this stage, sound effects such as speech or music can be added.

One of the best-known films made with the stop-motion technique was The Nightmare Before Christmas (1993), by Henry Selick, with a screenplay by Tim Burton. Chicken Run (2000) by Peter Lord and Nick Park, Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit (2005) by Steve Box and Nick Park, Coraline (2009) by Henry Selick, Fantastic Mr. Fox (2009) by Wes Anderson, as well as Mad Monster Party? (1967), Corpse Bride (2005) and Frankenweenie (2012), directed respectively by Jules Bass, Henry Selick and Tim Burton, are examples of stop-motion films. It was also used in the 1979 season openings of the series El Chavo del Ocho and El Chapulín Colorado. Several branches of filmmaking use this technique, but it is used mainly in animation work.

information.contentTitle: Credited As: Stop Motion Animator

content_list.content_text: Portugal also has some stop-motion animations, or true "animated puppets," the most relevant in recent times being the award-winning short film A Suspeita (The Suspicion) by José Miguel Ribeiro. The movement characteristics are unstable.

Stop-motion films can be made at home using just "miniatures"; they can be a simple pastime, since they always use little figures and since this type of animation attracts more attention from young audiences.

This technique has also been used to teach students concepts and techniques of basic education. The work of Koun-Tem, Chun-Huang and Ming-Chi showed that this practice is useful as a media literacy strategy. Stop motion is also widely used in Garry's Mod videos, which usually feature elements from Team Fortress 2, Half-Life 2 and Left 4 Dead.

information.contentTitle: The Making Of The Nightmare Before Christmas

content_list.content_text: Temperance melodramas, or Temperance Films, a specific genre that achieved great popularity until the end of the 1920s, aimed to combat alcohol consumption and support Prohibition. Pro-Prohibition propaganda films such as Prohibition (1915), directed by Hal Reid, Distilled Spirits (1915), directed by Milton J. Fahrney, and The Curse of Drink (1922), directed by Harry O. Hoyt, are examples of this genre.

information.contentTitle: Temperance propaganda film against alcohol (1920s)

content_list.content_text: A rotoscope is a device that allows animators to trace over film footage frame by frame for use in animation. It can be used to animate by following filmed reference. It can be considered a precursor of modern digital motion capture.

information.contentTitle: Max Fleischer's invention of the rotoscope

content_list.content_text: The device was invented by Max Fleischer, who used it in his Out of the Inkwell series starting in 1914. Fleischer had his brother, Dave Fleischer, dressed as a clown, serve as the reference footage for the character Koko the Clown. The rotoscope was later used in a wide range of cartoons, the most notable being Cab Calloway's dances in three Betty Boop cartoons from the early 1930s and the animation of Gulliver in Gulliver's Travels (1939).

Some purist animators scorn rotoscoping, but the technique often produces good results. When used as a reference tool for the animator, it can save a great deal of time. The Walt Disney Company used it effectively in Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, first in the animation of the Prince. By contrast, Ralph Bakshi used rotoscoping in a somewhat disparaging way in the animated films The Lord of the Rings (1978) and Wizards (1977) - and so he was able to produce animation without hiring animators. Rotoscoping as used by Bakshi is not much acclaimed by critics. The production company Filmation, founded in the 1960s, used the technique on a large scale, and it became known as the "Filmation style."

Low-quality rotoscoping has slight deviations in the line that show up in frame-by-frame playback, when the animation produces a "jittery" effect. Avoiding this "jitter" requires skill from whoever is applying the technique.

information.contentTitle: OUT OF THE INKWELL: Invisable Ink (1921)

content_list.content_text: Rotoscoping was frequently used as a tool for special effects in films. By tracing an object, a silhouette (known as a matte) can be created and used to make an empty space in the background of the scene. This allows objects to be placed into that scene. However, this technique has largely been replaced by chroma key. Rotoscoping has also been used to enable visual special effects guided by the matte or rotoscoped line.

A classic use of traditional rotoscoping is in the three original Star Wars films, where it was used to create the lightsabers by creating a silhouette based on the sticks held by the actors. The term "rotoscoping" is now used generally for the corresponding digital processes of drawing images over digital footage to produce mattes. This technique is still widely used in special cases where a blue screen cannot be used satisfactorily. Rotoscoping in the digital domain is often aided by motion tracking and onion-skinning software.

information.contentTitle: The trick that made animation realistic

content_list.content_text: Rotoscoping is often used to prepare matte cutouts for other matte-based processes. Richard Linklater produced a feature film using digital rotoscoping called Waking Life, creating a surreal image from the film's sequences, a technique also used in the production of A Scanner Darkly. The technique was also used to good effect in the 1980s music video for the song Take on Me, by the band A-ha.

list.title: What is Rotoscope Animation? The Process Explained

list.title: Animate reality with rotoscoping

content_list.content_text: CinemaScope was a filming and projection technology using anamorphic lenses, created by the president of Twentieth Century Fox in 1953. It was used between 1953 and 1967 to shoot widescreen films, marking the beginning of the modern format for both filming and exhibiting movies. The arrival of this anamorphic lens technology theoretically allowed the process to create an image with an aspect ratio of up to 2.66:1, almost twice as wide as the hitherto ubiquitous 1.37:1 format.

information.contentTitle: Watching Movie in CinemaScope, Letterbox vs conventional TV ratio

content_list.content_text: French professor Henri Chrétien developed and patented a new filming process he called Anamorphoscope in the late 1920s, which would become the basis of CinemaScope. Chrétien relied on lenses that use an optical trick, producing an image twice as large as that of conventional lenses. Later, in New York, a process similar to Chrétien's premiered, impressing the major Hollywood studios of the time, which were eager to win back audiences lost to the allure of television. Twentieth Century Fox bought the rights to the Anamorphoscope, but the format to be used still had to be defined. So Chrétien's first lenses were quickly shipped to Hollywood to be analyzed. From this analysis, the foundations of CinemaScope were laid.

information.contentTitle: The CinemaScope Story

content_list.content_text: Production of The Robe was halted so that the film could be made in CinemaScope, a technology that Fox president Spyros Skouras called "the future of cinema." With the introduction of CinemaScope, Fox and the other major studios would be able to reassert their distinction from their new competitor - television. CinemaScope was a film format used from 1953 to 1967. It aimed to keep TV from destroying the film industry. The standard was the basis for a revolution in the industry.

list.title: What is CinemaScope? Definition and Examples for Filmmakers

list.title: The rise of CinemaScope in the 1950s

content_list.content_text: Kinetic typography is the technical name for "moving text," a technique of animating text to express ideas using video animation. The text can be shown exactly at the moment it is spoken or sung, which makes it very useful for learning other languages.

With the advent of cinema and graphic animation came the possibility of combining text and motion. The first examples of animated lettering appeared in 1899, in the advertising work of Georges Méliès. In early films, most of the text was static. It was from 1960 onward that films began to open with titles displaying genuine kinetic typography. Scholars recognize that the first film to make extensive use of kinetic typography was Alfred Hitchcock's North by Northwest (1959).

It featured credit text that "flies" from top to bottom and from bottom to top, and finally disappears into the film itself. A similar technique was also used by Bass in Psycho (1960), also by Alfred Hitchcock. Since then, the use of kinetic typography has become common in film opening titles and television commercials. More recently, a common feature has been the use of numerous "idents" (identification clips) on television; one of the first idents was created by Martin Lambie-Nairn for the British television network Channel 4, in use since 1982.

Giallo (Italian for "yellow") is an Italian literary and film genre of suspense and crime fiction that peaked between the 1960s and the 1980s. The name refers to the yellow covers of Italian pulp magazines published from 1929 onward. The first film of the genre was Mario Bava's La ragazza che sapeva troppo (The Girl Who Knew Too Much), released in 1963, and one of the most recent is Dario Argento's Giallo, released in 2009.

information.contentTitle: What Is A Giallo Film?

content_list.content_text: There was a series of crime novels in Italy with yellow covers. When films began to be made about serial killers being hunted by detectives, the association with these books led to the film genre being nicknamed giallo. Most films in this genre are similar, featuring a serial killer (who is usually revealed only at the end; throughout the film we see only his hands in black leather gloves), a detective searching for the killer, shocking deaths, mainly of women (always with chase scenes before the act), and fully or partially nude bodies. Giallo was very important to the horror genre. Most of today's Italian filmmakers made their film debut with gialli. It was so popular in its day that it gave rise to the slasher genre (a serial killer stalking teenagers, very popular in the 1980s and 1990s) and the splatter genre (with a deliberate focus on graphic violence, usually containing scenes of mutilation, decapitation and lots of blood).

list.title: Where to begin with giallo

list.title: Murder, Italian Style: A Primer on the Giallo Film Genre

content_list.content_text: The slasher is a subgenre of horror film almost always involving psychopathic killers who kill at random. They are usually made on low budgets, which is why they are often labeled "B horror." The name slasher was coined because the basic premise of the film is a masked or costumed serial killer who racks up victim after victim throughout the film, until his mysterious identity is revealed by the protagonist who, after running for the entire film, ends up killing the villain.

information.contentTitle: A History of Slashers

content_list.content_text: Although the term is sometimes used colloquially as a catch-all for any horror film involving murders, genre analysts cite an established set of characteristics that allegedly set these films apart from other horror subgenres, such as splatter films and psychological horror films. Many films have stood out over the years since the genre took shape.

information.contentTitle: Evolution of the Slasher Genre

content_list.content_text: Its precursors were Tobe Hooper's The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974) and later John Carpenter's Halloween (1978), which brought with them the full potential of these films and their clichés.

list.title: The History of Slasher Movies
list.subtitle: liveabout.com

list.title: The History and Evolution of the Slasher Film
list.subtitle: vocal.media

content_list.content_text: The road movie is a film genre in which the main character(s) leave home on a journey, usually changing the perspective of their everyday life. These films usually depict journeys through the country's interior, exploring the theme of alienation and examining the tensions and issues of cultural identity of a nation or historical period; all of this is often entangled in a state of real or potential threat, lawlessness and violence, a "distinctly existential air," and these productions feature restless characters, "frustrated, often desperate." The setting includes not only the confines of the car as it moves along highways and roads, but also extends to diners and roadside motel rooms, which helps create intimacy and tension between the characters. Road movies tend to focus on the theme of masculinity (in which the man often goes through some kind of crisis), on some kind of rebellion and self-discovery. However, according to David Laderman's book Driving Visions: Exploring the Road Movie, the central theme of the genre is "transgression against conservative social norms."

information.contentTitle: Road Movie: Film Genres Converging on the Highway

content_list.content_text: There are two main narratives: the quest and the outlaw chase. In the former, the story moves forward as the characters make discoveries, which may be about themselves (for example, Two-Lane Blacktop, 1971); in the latter, in which the characters are fleeing the law, there is usually more sex and violence (for example, Natural Born Killers, 1994). Road movies also tend to focus more on the characters' inner conflicts and transformations —based on their feelings as they experience new realities on their journeys—, and a moment of silence is usually more important than a more dramatic sequence. The genre usually does not use the standard three-act structure of conventional films; instead, an "open-ended, rambling plot structure" is used.

information.contentTitle: Top 10 Travel Movies That Will Inspire Your Wanderlust

content_list.content_text: The name of the genre is also the title of the film Road Movie (1974), directed by Joseph Strick. Examples of this genre include Central Station, Crossroads, Motorista sem Limites, Easy Rider, Just Like the Son, Natural Born Killers, Rain Man, Thelma and Louise, Transamerica, The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert, Wild at Heart, Viagem sem Destino, Little Miss Sunshine, The Motorcycle Diaries, The Muppet Movie and Y tu mamá también.

content_list.content_text: In filmmaking, a set piece is a scene or sequence of scenes whose execution requires complex logistical planning and a considerable outlay of money. The term is also often used more broadly to describe a sequence in which the filmmaker's elaborate planning is meant to deliver the maximum payoff for the audience, such as a thrilling action sequence or an awe-inspiring science fiction sequence. The term is often used to describe any scenes so essential to a film that they cannot be cut or skipped in the shooting schedule without seriously harming the fun, intensity, impact and memorability of the final product. Screenplays are often written around a list of such set pieces, especially in high-budget blockbusters. The term is sometimes extended to refer to on-rails, quasi-cinematic sections of video games.

information.contentTitle: Mission: Impossible 4: Ghost Protocol- Crafting the perfect action set piece (Video Essay)

content_list.content_text: Set pieces are often meticulously planned using storyboards, screen tests and rehearsals, in contrast to smaller scenes in which the director and actors can improvise more. Each action requires the combined efforts of different departments: set builders, practical effects and special effects. On most films, different groups of people will work on different set pieces individually, since they can take a long time to prepare before shooting.

list.title: Filmmaking 101: Learn About the Role of Set Pieces in Screenwriting and Examples of Famous Set Pieces in Film
list.subtitle: Masterclass

content_list.content_text: Soft-core, or softcore, is a pornographic genre containing only nudity, sex and sexually suggestive scenes, but in which scenes (or photos) showing erect penises, penetration and ejaculation are prohibited. Softcore pornography is a form of cinematic or photographic pornography or erotica that is less sexually explicit than hardcore pornography. Its intent is to arouse the viewer, whether men or women. This genre of pornography depicts nude and semi-nude performers engaged in casual depictions of nudity or sexual intercourse or non-graphic masturbation. Softcore pornography excludes explicit depictions of vaginal or anal penetration, cunnilingus, fellatio and ejaculation. Visual depictions of the genitals (full nudity) are typically permissible in a softcore context in print media, and increasingly in film and television. Penile erections are not allowed, although attitudes toward this are changing.

Parts of the images considered too explicit may be obscured (censored) by various means. These techniques include the use of hair or draped clothing, carefully positioned hands or other body parts, precisely placed foreground elements in the scene (often plants or curtains), and carefully chosen camera angles. In most cases, the sexual acts depicted in softcore pornography are entirely simulated by the actors and actresses, with no actual penetration taking place. Actors often wear latex genital covers to avoid physical contact. Film directors go to great lengths to hide these covers on screen, but often cannot conceal them completely. In Brazil, this genre became popularly known through Brazilian cinema in the 1970s and 1980s, with the pornochanchada, and through the broadcasts of an erotic film slot on Rede Bandeirantes, "Cine Band Privé."

The drive-in theater is a moviegoing option in which the film is watched from inside the car, with the soundtrack usually transmitted over an FM radio frequency, or with speakers provided by the venue.

Until 2020, there was only one remaining example of this kind of movie theater in Brazil, the Cine Drive-in in Brasília. With the advent of the COVID-19 pandemic and the social isolation imposed to minimize the transmission of the virus, the drive-in theater reemerged in several cities across the country as a way to revive the sector, such as in the parking lot of the largest restaurant in Latin America, Madalosso in Curitiba, which opened one in June 2020. The comeback of the drive-in involved the development of new technologies to reduce physical contact.

The term is used to classify Australian exploitation films produced specifically in the '70s and '80s. Because it is not tied to a genre, Ozploitation is broad and encompasses films of the most varied themes, ranging from sexploitation and action to horror ("Patrick" and "Long Weekend" are two examples of Australian horror, part of Ozploitation, that were released by Versátil in the box set Obras-Primas do Terror vol. 11 (Masterpieces of Horror vol. 11)).

information.contentTitle: What is Ozploitation?

content_list.content_text: In 2008, Mark Hartley's documentary "Not Quite Hollywood: The Wild, Untold Story of Ozploitation!" popularized the term for good and showed the other face of films produced in Australia. Because many critics considered them "vulgar and offensive," Australian exploitation films ended up forgotten for years, disowned within the country's film history. Although Ozploitation is an offshoot of the Australian New Wave - and many films belong to both categories - it is important to note that not all Ozploitation belongs to the Australian New Wave (and vice versa).

list.title: Go Down Under with 20 Must-See Ozploitation Films!
list.subtitle: filmschoolrejects.com

content_list.content_text: Body horror, or biological horror, is a subgenre of horror film that intentionally presents graphic or psychologically disturbing violations of the human body. These violations may manifest through aberrant sex, mutations, mutilation, zombification, gratuitous violence, disease or unnatural movements of the body. Although it was originally applied to an emerging subgenre of American horror film, the concept of body horror has its roots in early Gothic literature and has expanded to include other media.

information.contentTitle: 54 body horror films explored

content_list.content_text: According to film scholar Linda Williams, body horror is one of three "gross" body genres, or "genres of excess," in cinema, the other two being pornography and melodrama. Williams writes that their success "is often measured by the degree to which the audience sensation mimics what is seen on the screen." For example, the viewer may experience feelings of fear through horror, sympathy through melodrama or sexual arousal through pornography. According to the book Horror Literature Through History, body horror "turns on the fear of the body and the limits of the flesh," and also "celebrates the transformative capabilities and potentialities inherent in the body. These bodily transformations are always ambiguous: violent and at the same time liberating, and repulsively beautiful."

information.contentTitle: Top 5 Scary Body Horror Movies That Are Hard To Watch

content_list.content_text: Body horror generally shares features with other horror subgenres, but it is different from them. For example, although elements of mutilation may be present in body horror, subgenres such as slasher, splatter or monster movies may also share this trope, but they differ in message and intent. A common difference in body horror is that violations or distortions of the body are rarely the result of immediate or initial violence. Instead, they are usually marked by a loss of conscious control over the body through mutation, disease or other tropes involving uncontrolled transformation. This subgenre can evoke intense feelings of physical and psychological revulsion, or disgust, in the viewer, and it explores anxieties about physical vulnerability.

information.contentTitle: The Fly - How To Make Body Horror

content_list.content_text: The term body horror was first used by Philip Brophy in his 1983 article "Horrality: The Textuality of the Contemporary Horror Film" to describe an emerging subgenre that arose during a short golden age of contemporary horror cinema focused on "bodily destruction" and "fear of one's own body." Although Brophy coined the term to describe a trend specifically within cinema, filmmaker Stuart Gordon notes that the body horror trope already existed before its adaptation to the screen, mainly in fiction.

Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) is one of the earliest examples of the subgenre in written fiction. The success of Gothic horror in the 19th century, combined with the rise of science fiction literature, is considered the origin of body horror as a literary genre. According to Halberstam: "By focusing on the body as the locus of fear, Shelley's novel suggests that it is people (or at least bodies) that terrify people (...), the landscape of fear is replaced by sutured skin."

content_list.content_text: An underground film is a film that is outside the mainstream, whether in its style, genre or financing.

The first printed use of the term "Underground Films" occurs in 1957, in American film critic Manny Farber's essay "Underground Films." Farber uses it to refer to the work of directors who "played an anti-art role in Hollywood." He contrasts "gangster-cowboy-war directors such as Raoul Walsh, Howard Hawks, William Wellman" and others with the "less talented De Sicas and Zinnemanns [who] continue to fascinate the critics." However, as with "Underground Press," the term developed as a metaphorical reference to a clandestine, subversive culture beneath the legitimate, official media.

In the late 1950s, "Underground Films" began to be used to describe the early independent filmmakers operating first in San Francisco, California, and New York, New York, and soon in other cities around the world. The movement was typified by the more experimental filmmakers working at the time, such as Shirley Clarke, Stan Brakhage, Harry Everett Smith, Maya Deren, Andy Warhol, Kenneth Anger, Jonas Mekas, Ken Jacobs, Ron Rice, Jack Smith, George and Mike Kuchar and Bruce Conner. By the late 1960s, the movement represented by these filmmakers had matured, and some began to distance themselves from the countercultural and psychedelic connotations of the word, preferring terms such as avant-garde or experimental to describe their work. Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, however, "Underground films" would still be used to refer to the more countercultural fringe of independent cinema.

"New Queer Cinema" is a term first used by academic B. Ruby Rich in Sight & Sound magazine in 1992 to define and describe a movement in independent cinema with "queer" themes in the early 1990s. The term developed from the use of the word queer in academic writing in the 1980s and 1990s as an inclusive way of describing the identity and experience of gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people, and also to define a form of sexuality that was fluid and subversive of the traditional understanding of sexuality. The main film studio to address these issues was fittingly named New Line Cinema, with its Fine Line Features division. Since 1992, the phenomenon has also been described by several other academics and has been used to describe various other films released since the 1990s. Films of the New Queer Cinema movement typically share certain themes, such as the rejection of heteronormativity and the lives of LGBT protagonists living on the margins of society.

content_list.content_text: Motion capture, or mocap, is a term used to describe the process of recording movement and transferring that movement onto a digital model. Originally invented in Scotland, the technique is used in military, entertainment, sports and medical applications.

content_list.content_text: In film productions, the term refers to recording the actions of human actors and using that information to animate virtual character models in 3D animation. When it includes the face and fingers, or captures subtle expressions, it is often referred to as performance capture.

content_list.content_text: Dogme 95 is an international film movement launched by a manifesto published on March 13, 1995, in Copenhagen, Denmark. Its authors were the Danish filmmakers Thomas Vinterberg and Lars von Trier. According to Vinterberg, the two took just 45 minutes to formulate the rules. They were presented a week later at the Odéon - Théâtre de l’Europe in Paris, on March 20, 1995, where von Trier had been invited to celebrate the centenary of the birth of cinema.

information.contentTitle: Dogma 95- The rules

content_list.content_text: The Dogme 95 Manifesto was written to create a more realistic and less commercial cinema. Later, two fellow Danes joined them, filmmakers Søren Kragh-Jacobsen and Kristian Levring. According to the filmmakers, it was an act of rescuing cinema as it was made before industrial exploitation (on the Hollywood model). The manifesto is both technical — setting out a series of restrictions on the use of techniques and technologies in the films — and ethical — with rules about the content of the films and their directors —, and its ideas are as controversial as its films.

The first film released with the certificate of compliance with the vow of chastity was Vinterberg's Dogme #1 – Festen (The Celebration, 1998), which was acclaimed by critics and received awards and nominations at film festivals. Owner of a company on the outskirts of Copenhagen, Zentropa Entertainment, von Trier released Dogme #2 – Idioterne (The Idiots, 1998), which also received awards and nominations. As the first two films to put the Dogme ideology into practice and to establish it as viable on the international film circuit, they had low production costs (around 1 million dollars) and a raw audiovisual language. The films have scenes so dark that at times you can't make out what is happening. In other scenes, the camera shakes so much that it leaves some viewers nauseous. There is also no concern with audio quality. None of these features would be the least bit appealing in a film by ordinary standards – but the plot alone would make it at least intriguing.

content_list.content_text: Splatter, or gore, is a subgenre of horror film that deliberately focuses on graphic depictions of blood and violence. Through the use of special effects, these films tend to display an evident interest in the vulnerability of the human body and its theatrical mutilation. The term "splatter cinema" was coined by George A. Romero to describe his film Dawn of the Dead (1978), although critics generally consider that film to have higher aspirations, as social commentary, than simply being exploitative for its own sake.

information.contentTitle: Top 10 der besten SPLATTER, GORE und EKEL-Szenen

content_list.content_text: In animation, several cartoons that show large amounts of blood and the characters' suffering as a form of comic humor can be classified in this subgenre, such as Family Guy, Happy Tree Friends and Mr. Pickles. Anime can also be classified as gore, but unlike Western cartoons, anime in this subgenre has a more serious/frightening atmosphere instead of a comedy-oriented setting.

In recent years, the combination of graphic violence and sexually suggestive imagery in some films has been labeled "torture porn" or "gorno" (a portmanteau of "gore" and "porno"), as with Cannibal Holocaust (1980). On the other hand, films such as Braindead (1992), and to some extent Dawn of the Dead, which feature over-the-top gore, can be interpreted as comedy and fall into the splatstick category.

content_list.content_text: Japanese horror, also called J-Horror, is a style of horror works produced in Japanese popular culture, renowned for its unique themes and for its distinctive treatment of the horror genre in light of Western approaches. Japanese horror tends to focus on psychological horror and the building of tension (anticipation), especially involving yūrei (ghosts) and poltergeists, while many works contain themes related to folk religion, such as possession, exorcism, shamanism, premonition and yōkai.

The origin of Japanese horror lies in the Edo and Meiji periods, when these stories were known as kaidan. The 1998 film Ring showed the image of the yūrei to the West for the first time; they are ghosts, spirits bound to the physical world by strong emotions that do not allow them to move on. Depending on the emotion that binds them, they manifest as a particular type of ghost. The most common type is the onryō, a ghost driven by a desire for revenge.

Like many creatures of folklore, such as werewolves and vampires, these ghosts follow certain rules: they are usually women (although there are male yūrei), wear white clothing (the color of funeral garments in Japan) and have long hair. Many Japanese horror films have had American remakes.

Found footage (known in Brazil as "Filmes Perdidos") is a film genre that emerged in the 1980s. It consists of a film posing as a documentary shot with a simple handheld camera. The style is often used for horror films. The style remains successful to this day.

content_list.content_text: The film that popularized the style was The Blair Witch Project, which was soon followed by a parody in the same style (Da Hip Hop Witch) starring Eminem and Vanilla Ice. However, the work that inaugurated the style was Cannibal Holocaust, an Italian film from 1980 directed by Ruggero Deodato. A long time passed before more films in this style appeared in theaters: in 2007, with Oren Peli's Paranormal Activity and [REC], by Jaume Balagueró and Paco Plaza, which spawned a remake the same year. The films became hits. A year later, Cloverfield was released, starring Michael Stahl-David and Odette Yustman. Instead of dealing with spiritual phenomena, it is about a monster attack in New York.

Then, in 2009, the sequel to Paranormal Activity, Paranormal Activity 2, and [REC]² were released. In 2010 came Paranormal Activity 2: Tokyo Night and The Fourth Kind, starring Milla Jovovich, the first to focus on aliens. In 2011, Apollo 18, the third installment of Paranormal Activity, Paranormal Activity 3, and the first Brazilian horror film, Desaparecidos, were released. And in 2012 came Chronicle, the first film of the genre about superheroes, and Project X, the first comedy of the genre - in addition to the fifth chapter of the Paranormal Activity series.
